live.name: BRONZE SATIN
live.headline: BRONZE SATIN: what the catalogue records about this tracked threat actor
live.in_short: BRONZE SATIN is Secureworks' name for an actor also tracked as HAFNIUM, Murky Panda and Silk Typhoon. The catalogue lists two web shell tools. No report card gives more detail.

sentences.t: BRONZE SATIN is the name used in the Secureworks entry for this threat actor.
The catalogue lists three other names for the same actor: HAFNIUM, Murky Panda and Silk Typhoon.
The catalogue lists two tools for this actor: ChinaChopper and Godzilla Webshell.

next.headline: BRONZE SATIN (HAFNIUM, Silk Typhoon): a China-linked espionage actor known for Exchange attacks
next.in_short: BRONZE SATIN is also tracked as HAFNIUM and Silk Typhoon. Governments and vendors link it to the 2021 Exchange attacks and, more recently, to supply-chain and remote-management intrusions. Several links come from named sources.

sentences.t: BRONZE SATIN is also tracked as HAFNIUM, Murky Panda and Silk Typhoon.
Microsoft Threat Intelligence describes Silk Typhoon as an espionage-focused Chinese state actor. It says it has tracked the group since 2020.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre judges it highly likely that HAFNIUM is associated with the Chinese state.
Microsoft says victims of the group's recent supply-chain activity were largely in state and local government and the IT sector.
BleepingComputer reports that the group has attacked defense contractors, policy think tanks, NGOs, healthcare, law firms and higher education in the United States, Australia, Japan and Vietnam.
The catalogue lists the China Chopper and Godzilla web shells among its tools.
A Wikipedia-derived summary says Hafnium used a JScript version of China Chopper in 2021 to exploit Exchange Server zero-days.
Microsoft reports stolen API keys used to reach downstream customer tenants, password spray with leaked credentials, and zero-day exploitation of edge devices and Exchange servers.
Microsoft says the group is not known to use its own dedicated infrastructure. It typically uses compromised covert networks, proxies and VPNs, likely to hide its operations.
Microsoft attributed the early-2021 exploitation of four Exchange zero-days to HAFNIUM. Microsoft released a patch on March 2, 2021.
The UK government said the Exchange compromise affected over a quarter of a million servers worldwide. The NCSC assessed it as highly likely that HAFNIUM was responsible.

In December 2022 the U.S. and allies attributed the Exchange campaign to hackers affiliated with China's Ministry of State Security. They named APT31 and APT40. Microsoft had earlier assessed HAFNIUM as exploiting the flaws.

BleepingComputer, citing Bloomberg, links Silk Typhoon to a breach of the U.S. Treasury's OFAC in early December 2024. The report says the attackers used a stolen BeyondTrust Remote Support API key. The attribution rests on Bloomberg and unnamed sources.
BleepingComputer relays Italian media reports that a Chinese national, Xu Zewei, was arrested in Milan on July 3 and is allegedly linked to Silk Typhoon. The report does not confirm that link.
Patch internet-facing servers quickly. Protect API keys and credentials for remote-management tools.
